lines.speaker: CLE
lines.text: This hand saved your life at the Granicus, Alexander! This hand!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Sit down, Cleitus. You're drunk.

lines.speaker: CLE
lines.text: Your father Philip won your wars for you! And now you dress like a Persian king!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Cleitus, stop! Alexander, he doesn't mean it!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Guards! Give me a spear!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alexander! No!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Samarkand, three hundred twenty-eight BC. The most powerful man on Earth has just killed one of his oldest friends.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I've known him since we were boys. We sat side by side, in the same classroom.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And your teacher was a man the whole world still knows. His name was Aristotle. To see how a boy became this, go back to the beginning.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Pella, the capital of Macedon. Three hundred forty-four BC. You're twelve, a nobleman's son, sent to the palace to serve the king.

lines.speaker: PHI
lines.text: Thirteen talents, for a horse that won't let anyone ride him? Take him away. He's useless.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Useless? You're losing a great horse, father, because nobody here knows how to handle him!

lines.speaker: PHI
lines.text: Ha! And you do, boy?

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: I do. And if I fail, I'll pay for him myself.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alexander, careful! He'll kick you!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Look. He's afraid of his own shadow. So I turn him, toward the sun.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Plutarch tells this story. Alexander turned the horse to face the sun, so he couldn't see his shadow, and then jumped on his back.

lines.speaker: PHI
lines.text: My son, find yourself a kingdom big enough for you. Macedon is too small.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The horse was called Bucephalus. Ox-head. He would carry Alexander all the way to India.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A year later, Philip hires the most brilliant mind in Greece to teach his son. Not in the city, but in a quiet place in the hills: the sanctuary of the nymphs, at Mieza.

lines.speaker: ARI
lines.text: Sit. Here, in the shade. Today, we talk about courage.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Courage is easy. You charge, and you never run.

lines.speaker: ARI
lines.text: Then a wild boar is the bravest creature alive. No. Courage lives in the middle, between running away, and running at death like a fool.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So, a brave man is still a little bit afraid?

lines.speaker: ARI
lines.text: Exactly. Too much is a mistake. Too little is a mistake. Good things live in the middle.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Aristotle really taught this. Today we call it the golden mean. Remember it. Your classmate is going to forget it.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: Alexander! Come on! Race you to the caves!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Hephaestion! You'll lose again!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Hephaestion. Alexander's closest friend, for the rest of his life. Ancient writers never list the whole class, so nobody knows for sure if he studied here.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The lessons covered politics, medicine, plants and animals, and Homer's poems.

lines.speaker: ARI
lines.text: Your copy of the Iliad. I corrected it myself. Read it like a soldier, not like a poet.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: I'll keep it under my pillow. Right next to my dagger.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Plutarch says he did exactly that, for the rest of his life.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Teacher. If I conquer the whole world, will you be proud of me?

lines.speaker: ARI
lines.text: I'll be proud if you can rule yourself. Conquering the world is the easy part.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You can still visit this school today. Near the town of Naousa, in northern Greece, the caves and the stone walkways are still there.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Three hundred thirty-six BC. King Philip celebrates his daughter's wedding in the theatre at Aegae.

lines.speaker: PHI
lines.text: Let the people see me! No guards. I'm among friends!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Who's that man? He's running at the king!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: One of Philip's own bodyguards, a man named Pausanias, stabbed him in front of the whole crowd.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: The king is dead! Philip is dead!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alexander. You're the king now. At twenty.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Then everyone who thinks I'm just a boy is about to learn something.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Soon after, in Corinth, the young king meets the strangest man in Greece: Diogenes, who lives in a big clay jar.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: I am Alexander, king of Macedon. Ask me for anything you want.

lines.speaker: DIO
lines.text: Then move a little to the side. You're blocking my sun.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: How dare you!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: No. If I were not Alexander, I would want to be Diogenes.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Did this really happen? Many ancient writers tell it. But it's so perfect that some historians think it was polished over the years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Spring, three hundred thirty-four BC. Alexander crosses into Asia with about thirty-five thousand men, against the largest empire in the world.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Watch.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He threw his spear into the beach! Why?

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: He's claiming it. All of Asia, won by the spear.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Diodorus writes that Alexander threw a spear into the shore of Asia before stepping off his ship. Today, that beach is in Turkey.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A few weeks later, at the river Granicus, the Persians are waiting on the other bank.

lines.speaker: PAR
lines.text: The river is deep, my king, and the banks are steep. Wait until tomorrow.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: I crossed the Hellespont, Parmenion. I'm not afraid of a stream. Follow me!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Alexander charges straight into the river. His helmet has two tall white plumes, so everyone can see him.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He's in front of everyone! They're all aiming at him!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A Persian noble splits Alexander's helmet with an axe. Another raises his sword for the final blow.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alexander! Behind you!

lines.speaker: CLE
lines.text: I've got him!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Cleitus, called the Black, cuts off the Persian's arm. He saves Alexander's life. Six years later, Alexander will kill him.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Gordion, in the middle of Anatolia. An old legend says: whoever unties this knot will rule all of Asia.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: Nobody can find the ends. People have tried for hundreds of years.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Then it doesn't matter how I untie it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Most writers say he cut it with his sword. But Aristobulus, who was there, says he simply pulled out the wooden pin that held it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: November, three hundred thirty-three BC. Issus, near today's Iskenderun. For the first time, Alexander faces the Persian king himself. Darius the Third.

lines.speaker: DAR
lines.text: They are so few. Surround them. Bring me that boy in chains.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Companions! There is the king! Ride with me!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He's going straight for Darius's chariot!

lines.speaker: DAR
lines.text: Turn the chariot! Turn it! Get me out of here!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Darius ran. He left behind his treasure, his tent, and his own family.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That evening, Alexander and Hephaestion visit the captured queen mother of Persia, Sisygambis.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Great king. Please. Have mercy on my family.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: My lady, I'm not the king. He is.

lines.speaker: SIS
lines.text: Forgive me! I didn't know! Forgive me!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: You made no mistake, mother. He is Alexander too.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Several ancient writers tell this story. And Sisygambis grew to love Alexander like a son.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Next, Alexander takes the whole coast. The island city of Tyre, after a seven-month siege. Then Egypt, where a priest in the desert oasis of Siwa calls him a son of the god Ammon.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Son of a god? Alexander, your father was Philip. I knew him.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Careful, my friend. A king can have more than one father.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: October, three hundred thirty-one BC. Gaugamela, in today's northern Iraq. Darius has gathered a giant army, and chariots with blades on their wheels.

lines.speaker: DAR
lines.text: Flatten the ground. My chariots need a smooth field.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But Alexander has the phalanx. Sixteen men deep, holding spears called sarissas, up to six meters long.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Chariots! Here they come!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Open the lines! Let them through!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The soldiers step aside. The chariots race into the gaps, and are cut down from behind.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: There! A gap in their line! Companions, with me!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Darius is running again!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Darius escaped. A few months later, his own nobles killed him. Alexander was now the king of Persia.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Persepolis. The most magnificent palace in the world, and now it belongs to Alexander.

lines.speaker: SOL
lines.text: Gold! The rooms are full of gold!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Plutarch says it took ten thousand pairs of mules and five thousand camels to carry the treasure away.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Then, one night, after a drinking party, the palace burns.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: Alexander, why? It's beautiful!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: The Persians burned Athens. Now Persia burns.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Was it revenge, or a drunken mistake? The ancient writers disagree.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He's wearing Persian robes now. He has Persian guards. Hephaestion, does he even remember Mieza?

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: He remembers. He just doesn't want to be that boy anymore.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And so we're back, on that night in Samarkand.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: What have I done? Cleitus. Cleitus!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: For three days, Alexander locked himself in his tent. He didn't eat. He didn't speak.

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: He won't talk to anyone. Not even me.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Remember what Aristotle said? Too much is a mistake. He's lost the middle.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A year later, Alexander asks his men to bow down before him, the Persian way.

lines.speaker: CAL
lines.text: In Greece, we bow only to the gods. I will not kneel to a man.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: You're Aristotle's own relative, Callisthenes. He taught you to argue. Not to obey.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Callisthenes was Alexander's official historian. Soon after, he was arrested, and died in captivity.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: First Cleitus. Now Callisthenes. Who's next?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Three hundred twenty-six BC. The army reaches India, at the river Hydaspes. On the other side, King Porus is waiting, with war elephants.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: What are those? They're as big as houses!

lines.speaker: HEP
lines.text: Elephants. The horses won't go near them.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So Alexander crossed the river at night, in a thunderstorm, far from Porus's camp.

lines.speaker: POR
lines.text: Elephants forward! Crush them!

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Spears up! Aim for the drivers!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: One's coming right at me! Shields! Shields!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The wounded elephants panic, and trample both armies. Porus fights on, wounded, until the very end.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: How do you want to be treated?

lines.speaker: POR
lines.text: Like a king.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Alexander was so impressed that he gave Porus his kingdom back, and more land on top of it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But soon after the battle, Bucephalus died, of old age and exhaustion. He was about thirty. Alexander named a city after him.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Further east! To the Ganges, and the end of the world. Just one more river.

lines.speaker: COE
lines.text: No, my king. Eight years we've followed you. Our fathers are dead. Our children don't know our faces. Let us go home.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Then go! Go home, and tell them you left your king among his enemies!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Once again, Alexander shut himself in his tent for three days. But the army didn't move. For the first time in his life, he turned back.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The way home crosses the Gedrosian desert, in today's Pakistan and Iran. The heat kills thousands of soldiers, women, and animals.

lines.speaker: SOL
lines.text: My king. We found a little water. It's for you.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Drink it, Alexander. You need it.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: If my men can't drink, then neither can I.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Arrian writes that Alexander poured the water into the sand, in front of the whole army. And it was as if every man had drunk.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A year later, in Ecbatana, Hephaestion falls ill with a fever. Within days, he's dead.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alexander. He's gone.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Then half of me is gone with him.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Babylon. June, three hundred twenty-three BC. After a long night of drinking, Alexander gets a fever. It doesn't go away.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alexander. Can you hear me? It's me.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: Remember Mieza? The shade. The caves. Aristotle and his long lessons.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I remember everything.

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: I wanted to be the greatest. Maybe I was. But I never learned the middle.

lines.speaker: SOL
lines.text: My king. Who gets the empire?

lines.speaker: ALE
lines.text: To the strongest.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Did he really say that? Some ancient writers report it. Others say he could no longer speak at all.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Alexander died in June, three hundred twenty-three BC. He was thirty-two. His generals fought over his empire for the next forty years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, how much of this really happened?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Here's the strange part. Every full history of Alexander that survives was written three to four hundred years after his death.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: But people were there! Didn't anyone write it down?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: They did. Ptolemy, Aristobulus, Callisthenes. But all their books are lost. We only have pieces of them, quoted by later writers.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And one famous line is a myth: that Alexander cried because there were no more worlds to conquer. Plutarch actually wrote the opposite. He cried because there were endless worlds, and he hadn't even conquered one.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And his tomb? It stood in Alexandria, in Egypt. Roman emperors visited it. Then it vanished. Nobody has found it to this day.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Twenty years. From a stone bench in Mieza, to the edge of India. And I was there for all of it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, if you'd been in that tent in Samarkand, would you have kept quiet? Or told him the truth, like Cleitus? Tell me in the comments.
